headline.main: Drones over Poland: NATO and the EU Seek a Convincing Response to Russian Aggression
headline.social: Drones over Poland: NATO and the EU Seek a Convincing Response to Russian Aggression

intro: Russia has continued to provoke NATO and the EU. The drone incursion into Polish airspace earlier this month has Western leaders scrambling for answers. Putin, meanwhile, has made it clear he won't be backing down any time soon.
text:
German troops monitor the airspace over Ukraine around the clock. Night after night, they see Russian drones deployed across the region, with increasing numbers recently turning up in the western part of the country.
On a recent Tuesday night dots began appearing on the troops’ radar screens – hardly unusual here in the southeastern corner of Poland at the Rzeszów airport. Germany’s military, the Bundeswehr, has stationed two Patriot anti-aircraft systems here since January. The border isn’t even 70 kilometers away. But on this night, there was something different.
Some of the points began moving toward Polish airspace and crossed the border into the NATO member state’s territory. The German soldiers passed along what they were seeing, contributing their radar data to the overall NATO surveillance regime as foreseen by the alliance’s air defense rules. Then, the alarm was triggered. Polish F-16 fighter jets and Dutch F-35 stealth warplanes scrambled, with the aircraft shooting down at least three of the more than 20 drones.
According to a NATO spokesperson, it marked the first time that Russian combat drones had been shot down over NATO territory.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin was immediately informed about the incident on NATO’s eastern front and Germany immediately established contact with the Polish government in Warsaw. The situation room in the Germany Foreign Ministry closely followed developments as did the Bundeswehr.
When Merz and his closest advisers came together in the Chancellery for their morning conference several hours later, the drones were the primary topic of conversation. The ensuing cabinet meeting also largely focused on what had happened over eastern Poland during the previous night. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius told the gathered ministers that it had been an unprecedented Russian provocation and that Russian strongman Vladimir Putin was testing NATO, as DER SPIEGEL later learned from meeting participants.
It wasn’t the first time that Russia had violated the airspace of a NATO ally. But with so many drones at once? At the same time? That was new. And it was an incident that marked a turning point – an escalation in the conflict with Russia.
How should NATO react? Should the alliance respond forcefully? Or would that risk triggering an unpredictable spiral that could spin out of control? That is the question that politicians, military leaders and diplomats in Berlin, Brussels and other Western capitals grappled with the next day and are still grappling with. The West’s cohesion, its determination, are needed more than ever. The test case of which senior Bundeswehr officers have long been warning internally has now arrived.
The West’s Dilemma
Ever since the beginning of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine more than three years ago, U.S. Presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and his successor Merz, and French President Emmanuel Macron have constantly emphasized that NATO cannot allow itself to be pulled into a conflict with the nuclear power of Russia. The alliance must not become a party to the war. For this reason, there has always been a certain reticence about supplying weapons to Ukraine – and it also why the West has thus far declined to commit ground troops to guarantee a future peace there.
But the drone incursions have plunged the West into a dilemma, and the incident has forced NATO’s hand. There has to be a response. What would it look like if NATO simply accepted Russia’s violation of an alliance partner’s territory with a shrug? Russia would likely see such a response as an invitation to additional provocations. And more aggression.
NATO has a framework of guidelines meant to ensure order in an emergency and to offer direction amid chaos. One of them is Article 5, which holds that an attack on one alliance member is an attack on the entire alliance. But before Article 5 comes Article 4: If a partner feels threatened, it can call the others together for consultation. Poland invoked Article 4 following the drone incursions. The last time this mechanism was activated was on February 24, 2022, the day of Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk expressed the urgency of the situation on the day after the incident. He has no cause to claim that his country was on the brink of war, Tusk said on that Wednesday morning, "but a line has been crossed” and things had grown more dangerous. "This situation brings us the closest we have been to open conflict since World War II.”
That Wednesday, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was scheduled to appear before the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, for a question-and-answer session. The appearance had been scheduled long before, but it now gave Pistorius the opportunity to discuss how he sees the situation in Poland.
There is no reason to believe, Pistorius said, that the incursions were made in error. "These drones were very clearly guided onto this course. They did not need to take this route to reach Ukraine.” Later, the minister doubled down: "There is absolutely no indication that these drones accidentally flew in such numbers along this route over Polish territory,” he said. The aircraft – either "Shahed or something similar” – took off from Belarus, he said. "You certainly don’t need to fly over that area to get from Belarus to Ukraine,” he said. It is therefore "reasonable to assume that this was a deliberate action.”
Not an accident, in other words. Intentional.
Pistorius and Bundeswehr leaders see the incident as confirmation of the warnings they have long been issuing about the threat posed by Russia. A short time later, Chancellor Merz said: "Russia endangered lives in a country that belongs to NATO and the EU. This brazen action is part of a long series of provocations in the Baltic region and along NATO’s eastern front.”
NATO believes the drones that flew in from Belarus were of the Shahed model or the Russian copy known as Gerlan, along with smaller Gerbera kamikaze drones. All of them were apparently armed with explosives. DER SPIEGEL has learned that NATO believes that at least five of them had the logistics center of Rzeszów as their target. The Dutch F-35 warplanes targeted those drones that were flying toward Rzeszów. The airport there is one of the most important hubs for weapons deliveries and other military supplies to Ukraine.
The operation aligns well with Putin’s pinprick strategy. Using low-level provocations, he tests the West’s defensive capabilities and sees how far he can go. Russia’s military involvement is limited, but the effect – the uncertainty such actions sow – is considerable.
Putin’s Message
The swarm of Russian drones is a blatant threat to Europe: Putin is expressing his willingness to escalate the war in Ukraine and to extend it beyond Ukraine’s borders. Recently, Putin has repeatedly made his opposition clear to the idea of a so-called coalition of the willing that would see Western troops securing a potential peace agreement in Ukraine. The drone incursion may have been a warning to not continue pursuing such a plan. Putin very clearly wants to create the impression that he would not shy away from a confrontation with NATO.
Putin sees himself in a position of strength and appears convinced of Russia’s superiority. Ever since the Alaska summit in mid-August with U.S. President Donald Trump, he has launched increasingly intense drone and missile attacks against Ukraine, most of them targeting civilian institutions. On one single night in late August, 25 people were killed in Kyiv when missiles crashed into the city center. The British Council offices and the EU representation in the city were also damaged. On a recent Saturday night, Russia then sent a record number of 810 drones into Ukraine. An Iskander ballistic missile even set the Ukrainian government’s main building on fire.
And Moscow recently held an additional show of strength in the form of a joint military exercise with Belarus known as Zapad. The exercise took place from September 12 to 16 and involved several thousand soldiers on Belarusian territory. The word "Zapad” means West. Poland and the Baltic countries were watching closely.
Meanwhile, the leadership in Moscow isn’t even trying to seriously reject the accusations coming from Warsaw. As usual, the Kremlin is playing for time. "No evidence has been presented that these drones are of Russian origin,” said the charge d’affaires of the Russian Embassy in Warsaw. Putin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said that Warsaw had not contacted Moscow in the wake of the incident. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Telegram on the Wednesday following the incident that the drones had been heading for targets in Ukraine and not in Poland. The maximum range of the drones used in the attack, Russia said, allegedly does not exceed 700 kilometers. Moscow said it would be willing to hold consultations with Poland. All of them vague, noncommittal statements.
So what happens next?
Boosting Defenses
NATO has significantly strengthened its air defenses on its eastern flank since the incursions, including additional Patriot air defense systems from the Netherlands. But the Bundeswehr has no illusions about the military’s defense capabilities should it be attacked by drones. "One of our greatest weaknesses is defending against drones,” said Alfons Mais recently, the outgoing Army Inspector, Germany’s senior-most military post. The Bundeswehr has ordered systems like the Skyranger from Rheinmetall, which can shoot down drones at short range, Mais said, but production takes time. As such, gaps in the military’s anti-drone defenses will persist for some time. "The question, though, is: Do we have that time?” Mais said. The incursions over Poland would suggest not.
The Ukrainian government has long been urging NATO to deploy its anti-aircraft defenses to shoot down drones over Ukraine as well. Kyiv has been using the incident in Poland to press its case. "Ukraine has long been calling on its partners to create a joint air defense system,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on the day after the incursion. Recently, he has become more vociferous, saying earlier this week on Telegram that: "Now is the time to implement a joint defense of our European sky with a multilayer air defense system.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has likewise been blunt: "This situation shows that finally the decision needs to be taken to enable partner air defense capabilities in neighboring countries to be used to intercept drones and missiles in Ukrainian airspace,” he wrote on X. A weak NATO response, he wrote, would simply provoke Russia: "And then Russian missiles and drones will fly even further into Europe.”
But it is questionable whether NATO will now expand its air defenses to Ukrainian airspace. When asked directly about the possibility, Pistorius merely said: "We are not speculating on that.”
Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, chair of the Defense Committee in European Parliament, has called on the West to produce a decisive response. "Otherwise, the countries that share a border with Russia and which depend on NATO will lose their faith in the alliance. And that is exactly what Putin wants. NATO must react now.”
But how? Because there is a clear lack of appetite for a military escalation with Russia, the EU could take the lead. What that might look like was sketched out by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. On Wednesday morning, mere hours after the drone incursions in eastern Poland, von der Leyen was in European Parliament in Brussels to deliver her "State of the Union” address as planned. The speech is her most important address of the year, and it was quickly adjusted to reflect that morning’s incident. The serious expression on her face matched the mood. "Europe is in a fight,” she began. "A fight for a continent that is whole and at peace. A fight for our values and democracies.”
Von der Leyen left no doubt about the fact that she sees Putin as the greatest threat to those values. The drone incursion, she said, was a "reckless and unprecedented violation of Poland’s and Europe’s air space.” Von der Leyen then added: "Europe stands in full solidarity with Poland.” The gathered lawmakers stood and applauded.
The Commission president also announced plans to make 6 billion euros available for a partnership with Ukraine to produce drones. The money is to come from a loan that will be repaid with interest generated from frozen Russian assets. "This is Russia’s war. And it is Russia that should pay.”
Von der Leyen also proposed a new program for providing military support to Ukraine, intended to give the country a qualitative military advantage. The eastern flank of the EU must also be further strengthened, she said. "We must invest in real-time space surveillance,” she said, "so that no movement of forces goes unseen.” Beyond that, she intoned, it is time to listen to the Baltic nations and build a "drone wall.” Doing so, she said, "is not an abstract ambition. It is the bedrock of credible defense.”
Von der Leyen struck a forceful tone and chose strong words – perhaps also to conceal Europe’s uncertainty and underlying unease.
In Berlin and other European capitals, there is likely some hope that Russian drones flying over the border into Poland may also be enough to convince U.S. President Trump to change his tune. That Trump will abandon his dream of negotiating a deal with Putin and instead strengthen sanctions against Russia to force Moscow to the negotiating table.
Behind the scenes, the European Commission is working on new sanctions against Russia. EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan was recently in Washington for talks, which apparently went well according to sources in the EU. Washington, they said, is prepared to increase the pressure on Russia by upping the pressure on China and India, both of which have become important trading partners for Moscow. Experts from the EU and the U.S. continue to work toward ironing out the details.
But whether the U.S. will really impose stronger sanctions against China and India remains to be seen, and if so, when. Trump has expressed surprise about the incident in Poland. "What’s with Russia violating Poland’s airspace with drones? Here we go!” Trump wrote on his network Truth Social.
It was Mark Rutte of all people, the NATO secretary general, who laid bare the West’s uncertainty about how to move forward. "Stop it!” Rutte said in a comment intended for Putin, and it sounded almost as though he was begging. Putin, Rutte said, shouldn’t just stop violating NATO airspace, but the entire war in Ukraine.
For now, though, that is nothing more than wishful thinking.
